chunks: BJT I-V characteristic curves. The question: Draw IV curve.
The BJT output curves are a graph that shows how a transistor behaves across its whole range. The horizontal axis is the voltage across the transistor, V CE .
The vertical axis is the collector current. You draw several curves, one for each value of base current.
Each curve rises quickly, then flattens, and a bigger base current gives a higher curve.
Picture a water tap feeding a tank. Turn the tap handle to a chosen setting, and the flow quickly rises and then stays steady no matter how the water pressure changes.
Each handle setting gives a different steady flow. The handle is the base current, and the steady flow is the collector current.
The analogy breaks down in one place: real curves tilt up slightly, from the Early effect.
The family of output curves. Saturation is the steep region near the origin (the tanh factor is a smooth stand-in for the sharp knee; real curves bend over by about 0. 2 volts).
In forward-active the curves are nearly flat and evenly spaced, with I C about beta I B , and a gentle upward tilt from the Early effect.
The dashed load line crosses the 40 microamps curve at about 4. 2 milliamps and 5.
8 volts; its two ends mark cutoff (right, V CE equals V CC , I C equals 0 ) and saturation (left, I C equals V CC over R C ). Breakdown at higher V CE is not drawn.
Drag I B up to 100 microamps: β·I B reaches the 10 milliamps the load line can supply, so Q slides down to the saturation knee at the left.
Drag R C up and the same happens at a smaller base current.
Output characteristic: collector current versus V CE , one curve per base current. Saturation region: the steep part at low V CE , where the transistor is fully on.
Forward-active region: the flat part, where I C about beta I B . Early effect: the slight upward tilt of the flat part as V CE rises.
Load line: a straight line showing which operating points the external circuit allows.
Use the example from further down this page. Say beta equals 100 . A base current of 40 microamps gives a flat curve at I C equals 100 times 40 micro A equals 4 milliamps.
Use a 10 volts supply and a 1 kilohms collector resistor. The load line runs from 10 volts on the voltage axis to 10 milliamps on the current axis.
At 4 milliamps, the resistor drops 4 volts, so V CE equals 10 minus 4 equals 6 volts. That is the whole idea.
"The BJT output curve plots collector current against collector-emitter voltage for stepped base currents.
Each curve rises steeply near the origin in saturation, then goes nearly flat in the forward-active region at I C about beta I B with a slight Early-effect slope, and breaks down at high V CE .
The input curve is a diode, with a knee near 0. 65 volts, and the transfer curve is exponential, a decade per 60 millivolts.
A load line across the output curves gives the operating point."
